distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for alcohol-associated hepatic steatohepatitis with jaundice and inflammatory liver dysfunction. Acute liver failure, cholangitis, viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, decompensated cirrhosis, pancreatitis, sepsis, malignancy, and biliary obstruction remain mimics or context, not disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use harmful alcohol exposure, recent alcohol escalation or withdrawal context, jaundice, hepatomegaly or tender liver, AST-predominant transaminitis, high GGT, direct-predominant hyperbilirubinemia, INR/PT, albumin, leukocytosis, macrocytosis, portal-hypertensive findings, ascites, encephalopathy, and renal or infection hazards. Liver biopsy, exclusion of viral/autoimmune/biliary/DILI mimics, final paper diagnosis, treatment response, and outcome should be confirmatory/non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Alcohol metabolite oxidative and mitochondrial stress
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Sustained or recently escalated alcohol exposure generates acetaldehyde adducts, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, CYP2E1 induction, and altered gut-liver signaling that prime hepatocyte injury.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, and Mallory-type injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hepatocytes accumulate fat, swell, develop cytoskeletal injury, and release AST-predominant enzymes with a typical alcohol-associated hepatocellular pattern.

Damaged hepatocytes, endotoxin, DAMPs, IL-8/CXCL signals, and complement recruit neutrophils and amplify systemic inflammatory response, leukocytosis, fever, and CRP without requiring bacterial infection.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Canalicular cholestasis and bile excretory dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Alcohol-associated hepatocyte swelling, cholestasis, ductular reaction, and inflammatory bile transport impairment produce direct-predominant hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, high ALP, and high GGT.

Inflammatory hepatic dysfunction, low reserve, fibrosis/cirrhosis context, and sinusoidal pressure impair clotting-factor synthesis and albumin production, producing INR elevation, edema, ascites, portal-hypertensive physiology, and bleeding susceptibility.

Severe alcoholic hepatitis combines systemic inflammation with impaired neutrophil/macrophage function, gut permeability, aspiration risk, and malnutrition, raising infection and sepsis hazards and modulating steroid safety.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Hepatic encephalopathy, renal injury, and multiorgan failure cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe liver dysfunction, ammonia handling failure, inflammation, vasodilation, infection, GI bleeding, dehydration, and hepatorenal physiology can produce encephalopathy, AKI, shock, respiratory failure, and death.

Alcohol cessation, nutrition, infection control, and preserved hepatic reserve allow inflammation and cholestasis to recede; low activity represents poor regenerative reserve or continued alcohol injury.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Harmful alcohol exposure is the upstream context for alcoholic hepatitis.
Recent escalation or binge exposure can precipitate symptomatic alcoholic hepatitis.
Alcohol metabolite and oxidative injury drive steatosis and ballooning degeneration.
Hepatocyte injury releases inflammatory signals that recruit neutrophils.
Ballooning and canalicular injury impair bile excretion.
Severe inflammation impairs hepatic synthetic function and worsens portal-hypertensive decompensation.
Synthetic dysfunction and portal hypertension amplify encephalopathy, bleeding, renal, and shock pathways.
Infection in severe alcoholic hepatitis can precipitate renal failure, encephalopathy, shock, and death.
Sustained abstinence removes the ongoing alcohol injury driver.
Recovery capacity lowers bilirubin and cholestatic burden over days to weeks.
Alcohol induction and cholestasis commonly raise GGT.
Alcohol exposure and folate deficiency commonly cause macrocytosis.
Alcohol-associated hepatocyte and mitochondrial injury raises AST.
ALT rises but is often lower than AST in alcoholic hepatitis.
AST predominance is a common alcohol-associated transaminase pattern.
Steatosis and inflammation enlarge the liver.
Capsular stretch and inflammation cause tender hepatomegaly or RUQ pain.
Alcoholic hepatitis often appears with fatty liver or hepatomegaly on imaging.
Neutrophilic inflammation can produce marked leukocytosis or leukemoid reaction.
Alcoholic hepatitis leukocytosis is typically neutrophil-predominant.
Severe inflammatory stress may include bandemia after infection is excluded or as competing context.
Systemic inflammation raises CRP.
Fever may occur from sterile inflammation, infection, or alcohol withdrawal context.
Inflammation, withdrawal, pain, anemia, hypovolemia, or infection raise heart rate.
Alcoholic hepatitis is often clinically recognized by jaundice and high bilirubin.
Canalicular dysfunction produces conjugated bilirubin elevation.
Visible jaundice and scleral icterus reflect bilirubin burden.
Cholestasis can cause generalized pruritus.
ALP may rise with cholestatic alcoholic hepatitis, though marked biliary obstruction remains a mimic.
Reduced clotting-factor synthesis prolongs INR and contributes to severity scores.
Inflammation, impaired synthesis, malnutrition, and dilution lower albumin.
Severe alcoholic hepatitis can produce portal-hypertensive ascites even without established cirrhosis.
Sinusoidal inflammation and low reserve raise portal pressure.
Bilirubin and PT prolongation are combined in Maddrey severity scoring.
Bilirubin, INR, creatinine, and sodium contribute to MELD/MELD-Na severity.
Severe alcoholic hepatitis and steroid exposure increase infection risk.
Liver dysfunction and shunting raise ammonia in encephalopathy contexts.
Encephalopathy, alcohol withdrawal, infection, or metabolic disturbance can alter mental status.
West Haven grade captures hepatic encephalopathy severity.
AKI or hepatorenal physiology raises creatinine in severe alcoholic hepatitis.
AKI is a major mortality pathway.
Vasodilation, infection, bleeding, or dehydration can lower perfusion pressure.
Impaired hepatic clearance, hypoperfusion, or sepsis raises lactate.
Coagulopathy, portal hypertension, varices, gastritis, and thrombocytopenia increase GI bleeding risk.
Inflammation and cirrhosis/portal-flow context can increase portal venous thrombosis risk.
Encephalopathy, AKI, shock, respiratory failure, and sepsis are major near-term mortality pathways.
Infection is a major determinant of survival and steroid net benefit.
Abstinence and recovery capacity lower ongoing injury and death risk.

axes.shape_free_text: Heavy, sustained, or clinically harmful alcohol use context; quantity and chronicity are case evidence, not disease-name qualifiers.
Recent escalation, binge, relapse, or abrupt reduction after heavy use near presentation.
Risk or active context of alcohol withdrawal after recent cessation or reduced intake.
Visible jaundice, scleral icterus, dark urine, or generalized yellow discoloration.
Generalized itching from cholestatic bilirubin/bile-acid burden.
Fatigue, malaise, weakness, or reduced activity during alcoholic hepatitis.
Poor appetite, anorexia, or reduced intake.
Nausea, vomiting, retching, or poor oral tolerance.
Right upper quadrant, epigastric, or diffuse abdominal pain. Severe focal biliary or pancreatic patterns remain mimic/context evidence.
Tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, or liver capsule discomfort.
Palpable or imaging hepatomegaly from fatty enlarged inflamed liver.
Ultrasound, CT, MRI, or biopsy-compatible fatty liver/steatosis signal.
Clinical or imaging ascites, abdominal distension with fluid wave, or paracentesis-confirmed ascites.
Portal-hypertensive physiology from ascites with high SAAG, collateral/recanalized umbilical vein, varices, splenomegaly, or portal-flow imaging.
Palpable or imaging splenomegaly, usually portal-hypertension or hematologic context.
Imaging-confirmed portal venous thrombus in the alcoholic hepatitis context; remains a complication/context axis, not a separate disease-name qualifier.
Confusion, slowed speech, disorientation, somnolence, agitation, or coma from hepatic encephalopathy, withdrawal, infection, or metabolic context.
West Haven or equivalent hepatic encephalopathy grade.
Temperature may be normal or high from alcoholic hepatitis SIRS, infection, aspiration, or withdrawal.
Heart rate rises with inflammation, withdrawal, anemia, hypovolemia, pain, sepsis, or bleeding.
Perfusion pressure; low values mark bleeding, infection, vasodilation, or hepatorenal/shock context.
Respiratory rate may rise with infection, aspiration, ascites, encephalopathy, metabolic stress, or shock.
AST in alcoholic hepatitis is typically elevated but often below the thousands; AST commonly exceeds ALT.
ALT is elevated but often lower than AST in alcoholic hepatitis; very high ALT suggests viral/toxic/ischemic mimics.
AST/ALT ratio; values above one and often above two support alcohol-associated pattern but are not diagnostic alone.
ALP can be normal, mildly elevated, or markedly elevated in cholestatic alcoholic hepatitis; biliary obstruction remains a mimic/context.
GGT is often high with alcohol exposure and cholestasis.
Total bilirubin is a core jaundice/severity axis in alcoholic hepatitis.
Direct bilirubin is often prominently elevated with alcoholic hepatitis cholestasis.
Albumin falls with impaired synthesis, inflammation, dilution, malnutrition, and chronic reserve limitation.
INR rises with hepatic synthetic dysfunction and drives severity scores.
Maddrey discriminant function from bilirubin and prothrombin time; high values mark severe alcoholic hepatitis context.
MELD or MELD-Na severity score from bilirubin, INR, creatinine, and sodium.
Sodium may be low with advanced portal hypertension, ascites, low solute intake, or severe illness.
Creatinine rises with AKI, hepatorenal physiology, hypovolemia, infection, or shock.
BUN may rise with dehydration, renal injury, catabolism, or GI bleeding.
Ammonia can be elevated in hepatic encephalopathy but may not correlate perfectly with mental status.
Lactate may rise from impaired hepatic clearance, hypoperfusion, infection, seizure, or severe systemic inflammation.
Anemia may reflect chronic alcohol use, nutrition, GI bleeding, inflammation, or hemolysis context.
MCV is often high from alcohol exposure, folate deficiency, or liver disease.
Leukocytosis is common and can be extreme in leukemoid reaction; infection and malignancy remain mimics/context.
Neutrophil percentage or neutrophil predominance in alcoholic hepatitis inflammatory response.
Band forms may rise with severe inflammatory stress, infection, or leukemoid reaction.
Platelets may be normal, low from portal hypertension/alcohol marrow toxicity, or high/reactive; severe thrombocytopenia points to broader differential.
CRP rises with alcoholic hepatitis systemic inflammation and rises further with infection.
Ferritin can rise from inflammation, liver injury, alcohol-associated iron handling changes, or iron overload mimic context.
Melena, hematemesis, hematochezia, occult bleeding, or suspected GI bleeding in portal-hypertension/alcohol gastritis context.
Hazard of portal venous thrombosis in severe inflammatory/portal-hypertensive context.
Hazard of clinically important GI bleeding from portal hypertension, gastritis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or anticoagulation context.
Hazard of bacterial infection or sepsis during severe alcoholic hepatitis, especially with immune paresis or corticosteroid exposure.
Hazard of AKI or hepatorenal physiology from severe liver disease, infection, dehydration, bleeding, or shock.
Hazard of progression to acute-on-chronic or acute liver failure physiology; this is an event hazard, not the disease leaf name.
Lifespan mortality hazard for alcoholic hepatitis emerging from severity, infection, renal failure, encephalopathy, bleeding, shock, and recovery capacity.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Alcohol exposure and cholestasis commonly raise GGT.
AST and ALT usually rise together, with AST often higher.
AST predominance raises the AST/ALT ratio.
Bilirubin is a major MDF component.
Low albumin and portal pressure support ascites formation.
Portal hypertension is a major driver of ascites.
Very high WBC can be sterile AH inflammation but still raises the need to evaluate infection.
Creatinine rise marks AKI or hepatorenal risk.
Renal failure sharply worsens alcoholic hepatitis survival.
Infection and sepsis dominate severe alcoholic hepatitis mortality.
Higher encephalopathy grade signals severe liver dysfunction and aspiration/ICU risk.
GI bleeding can precipitate shock, encephalopathy, infection, and death.
Portal venous thrombosis can worsen portal flow and collateral/ascites physiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Withdrawal risk requires benzodiazepine or phenobarbital protocols, monitoring, and thiamine before glucose.
Encephalopathy and withdrawal can overlap clinically.
Encephalopathy increases aspiration risk and may require tube feeding precautions.
Ascites requires balancing nutrition with sodium restriction and volume status.
Wernicke risk should be covered when confusion occurs in alcohol-use context.

treatments.treatment_name: Prednisolone for severe alcoholic hepatitis context

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroid net benefit is considered in severe presentations.
Uncontrolled infection can make corticosteroids harmful.
Active GI bleeding is a major caution context.
Renal failure marks poor prognosis and changes net benefit.
NAC is often considered when severe liver failure physiology overlaps.

treatments.treatment_name: Lactulose and rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy context

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Higher encephalopathy grade increases urgency of ammonia-lowering and airway monitoring.
GI bleeding can precipitate encephalopathy and must be controlled.
AKI or hepatorenal physiology limits diuresis and favors albumin/paracentesis strategy.
Hyponatremia constrains fluid and diuretic management.

treatments.treatment_name: Infection screening, source control, and active antibiotics when infection context is present

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibiotic/source-control benefit depends on actual infection context.
Shock physiology needs parallel hemodynamic support.

treatments.treatment_name: Anticoagulation for portal vein thrombosis context

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anticoagulation is relevant when thrombosis is present or strongly suspected.
Varices, bleeding, and severe coagulopathy constrain anticoagulation.

treatments.treatment_name: Early liver transplant evaluation for selected nonresponse context

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rescue transplant evaluation is relevant in high predicted mortality and poor native recovery.
Transplant feasibility depends on structured psychosocial/addiction assessment rather than a diagnosis label.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Observed harmful alcohol exposure directly raises disease-context evidence.
GGT is alcohol-inducible and cholestasis-sensitive.
Alcohol and folate deficiency increase macrocytosis.
Recent escalation can precipitate symptomatic alcoholic hepatitis.
Recent injury can raise transaminases.
Malnutrition and inflammation lower albumin.
Poor nutritional reserve limits hepatic recovery.

treatment_effect_modulation.enteral_nutrition_high_protein_calorie_r: stronger when malnutrition or low intake context is active

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Baseline portal hypertension makes ascites and bleeding more likely.
Cirrhosis and portal pressure amplify ascites.
Low hepatic reserve worsens coagulopathy.
Infection is common and hazardous in severe alcoholic hepatitis.
Infection can add to sterile AH leukocytosis.

treatment_effect_modulation.prednisolone_for_severe_alcoholic_hepati: reduced or unsafe until infection is controlled
treatment_effect_modulation.infection_screening_source_control_activ: stronger when infection context is active

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Renal dysfunction raises creatinine and MELD.
AKI is a core severe AH complication.
Renal failure worsens prognosis.
Observed GI bleeding raises bleeding activity.
Portal hypertension and coagulopathy raise bleeding risk.
GI bleeding can precipitate encephalopathy.

treatment_effect_modulation.prednisolone_for_severe_alcoholic_hepati: reduced while active bleeding is uncontrolled
treatment_effect_modulation.portal_vein_thrombosis_anticoagulation_c: limited when bleeding hazard is high

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Continued alcohol sustains hepatocyte injury.
No abstinence blunts recovery.
Continued alcohol increases recurrent injury and mortality.

supportive_care: Keep the first-layer leaf name pure: Alcoholic hepatitis. Acute liver failure, cholangitis, viral hepatitis, DILI, decompensated cirrhosis, pancreatitis, sepsis, portal vein thrombosis, and malignancy are mimics, complications, or context axes.

Do not use final diagnosis, liver biopsy, negative viral/autoimmune/biliary workup, steroid response, abstinence response, or outcome as presentation-ranking evidence unless running a post-workup diagnostic mode.

Preserve presentation evidence even when it overlaps mimics: fever, leukocytosis, high CRP, ascites, GI bleeding, portal vein thrombosis, elevated ferritin, lactate, and cholestatic labs remain structured evidence.
Severity and treatment should emerge from bilirubin, INR/PT, creatinine, sodium, encephalopathy, infection, bleeding, MDF/MELD, and mortality hazard rather than from clinical ordering labels.
Corticosteroid behavior must be modulated by infection, GI bleeding, renal failure, and severity context; do not encode a universal treatment ordering label.
Alcohol exposure is a context/risk axis for this disease, not a generic reason to force every liver or abdominal case into this manifold.
